# The 100,000 most popular domains, as a canary list: no trail may match one of these.
#
# IN RANK ORDER, most popular first, and that is load-bearing - not a stylistic choice. The `:N`
# suffix on --canaries takes the first N LINES, so gate.yml reads this one file at two depths. Sort
# it alphabetically and `:30000` silently becomes "every name beginning with a digit through c",
# which is not a depth at all; it was written that way once and the literal gate quietly changed
# from 14 findings to 19 completely different ones.
#
# TWO DEPTHS, because the two halves of the check have opposite noise profiles.
#
#   REGEX trails, all 100,000. Measured across the full top 1M, only three patterns ever match a
#   ranked domain and the FIRST hit is at rank #89,031 - so a pattern reaching this far is almost
#   certainly too loose, which is signal rather than noise. It caught one on the day this landed:
#   `^[a-z]{2}\-[a-z]{2,3}\.(top|club)$` in android_roamingmantis.txt, the unfixed sibling of the
#   pattern a customer reported, matching qu-in.top, my-ip.club, ru-vpn.top and go-vpn.club.
#
#   LITERAL trails, the first 30,000. Here depth costs noise directly: these lists rank by DNS
#   QUERY VOLUME, so a C2 with a big botnet earns its rank honestly. Measured over the gated piles -
#   10k: 1 hit, 20k: 9, 30k: 16, 50k: 32, then 100k: 90. The jump between 50k and 100k is where a
#   curated exception list stops keeping up, so 30k is the last depth whose findings are a sitting's
#   work. Correct-but-ranked trails go in tests/canaries-allow.txt, WITH a reason.
#
# suspicious/ is not gated on this at all: those piles exist TO name popular services whose use is
# itself the signal - ddns.net, ngrok.io, wix.com, ipify.org - so nearly every literal hit is there
# and every one is correct.
#
# WHY IT IS NOT REFRESHED BY A ROBOT. A stale canary list is wrong only in the harmless direction:
# a domain that was popular six months ago is still one that must never be flagged. Measured churn
# is 15.6 per cent per six months on the top 10k, and all staleness costs is coverage of names that
# became popular since. Regenerate by hand when it feels thin, and bump '# Refreshed:':
#
#     curl -sSL https://tranco-list.eu/top-1m.csv.zip -o /tmp/t.zip
#     python3 -c "import zipfile;z=zipfile.ZipFile('/tmp/t.zip');\
#       print(chr(10).join(l.split(',')[-1].strip().lower() \
#       for l in z.open(z.filelist[0].filename).read().decode().split(chr(10))[:100000]))"
#
# Tranco rather than Alexa (retired 2022) or Cisco Umbrella (raw DNS volume, junk-heavy): it is a
# 30-day average across several sources, built to resist manipulation, and still published.
#
# Source: Tranco daily list. Ranks stripped, order kept.
# check_trails.py reads the line below and says how old this is; bump it when you regenerate.
# Refreshed: 2026-08-27
